title: Vendor and Procurement
subtitle: Getting Value from External Partners
description: Navigate government procurement to select the right vendors and manage them effectively.

content.overview: Understanding the unique constraints and opportunities of government procurement. Government IT procurement differs fundamentally from private sector purchasing due to transparency requirements, competitive bidding rules, and public accountability. This module explores how DPI and government agencies navigate these constraints to achieve their objectives while maintaining fiscal responsibility and fairness.

keyPoints.title: Transparency and Accountability Requirements
keyPoints.description: Government procurement is subject to open bidding laws (such as competitive sealed bidding) where all qualified vendors must have equal access to opportunities. Decisions must be documented and defensible.
keyPoints.implications: Plan longer timelines (6-9 months typical), document all evaluation criteria upfront, and prepare for potential protests from unsuccessful bidders.

keyPoints.title: Competitive Sealed Bidding vs. Request for Proposal
keyPoints.description: CSB is used for well-defined goods/services where price is primary factor. RFPs allow for qualitative evaluation when requirements are complex or outcomes are uncertain. DPI often uses RFPs for digital transformation and system modernization work.
keyPoints.implications: Choose the procurement method based on requirement clarity and need for vendor innovation, not just cost optimization.

keyPoints.title: Public Records and Bid Protests
keyPoints.description: All procurement documents, bids, and evaluation results are public record. Unsuccessful vendors have legal right to protest decisions, often delaying contract award by 30-60 days.
keyPoints.implications: Document all evaluation decisions thoroughly. Ensure your evaluation criteria are objective and consistently applied. Anticipate and prepare responses to potential protests.

keyPoints.title: Budget and Appropriations Constraints
keyPoints.description: Government budgets are fixed and appropriated annually. Mid-year contract awards may need to fit remaining budget. Multi-year contracts require multi-year appropriation commitments.
keyPoints.implications: Align procurement timeline with budget cycles. Seek multi-year pricing commitments early. Plan for contingency if vendor costs exceed budget.

keyPoints.title: Vendor Ecosystem Maturity
keyPoints.description: Government technology vendor landscape varies by region and service type. Some areas have monopoly or duopoly vendors; others have thriving competitive markets. DPI assessments often reveal limited options for specialized services.
keyPoints.implications: Conduct early market research. Consider reserve contracting for women/minority-owned businesses. May need to unbundle requirements to create competition.

content.keyInsight: Government procurement is slower, more transparent, and more constrained than commercial procurement—but these constraints also create opportunities for vendors who understand the rules and for government agencies that strategically plan ahead. Success requires embracing the process rather than fighting it.

exercises.title: Procurement Method Decision Framework
exercises.description: Given three government IT scenarios (cloud migration, legacy system replacement, staffing augmentation), determine whether to use sealed bid or RFP and justify your choice based on requirement clarity and complexity.
exercises.scenario: You're advising a state health agency on procuring a new identity verification system. Vendors must integrate with existing legacy mainframe systems, but integration requirements are not fully understood. Some vendors may have innovative approaches that reduce future costs.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Recognize that RFP is appropriate when requirements are complex or vendor innovation is valuable; sealed bid is appropriate for well-specified needs.

content.overview: Defining clear, measurable requirements that vendors can propose against and that you can objectively evaluate. Poor requirements definition is the #1 cause of procurement failure in government. Requirements must balance specificity (to prevent gaming and subjectivity) with flexibility (to allow vendor innovation). DPI often helps agencies clarify vague requirements through facilitated workshops and competitive dialogue.

keyPoints.title: Separating Outcomes from Implementation
keyPoints.description: Outcome requirements describe what problem you're solving or what capability you need ('Reduce license verification processing time from 2 weeks to 2 days'). Implementation requirements specify how vendors must deliver ('Must use Java Spring Framework').
keyPoints.implications: Over-specifying implementation limits competition and locks you into vendor decisions. Balance outcome requirements (mandatory) with technical preferences (nice-to-have). This is especially important when DPI is helping agencies modernize legacy systems.

keyPoints.title: Functional vs. Non-Functional Requirements
keyPoints.description: Functional requirements describe what the system does (create account, process payment). Non-functional requirements describe qualities the system must have (performance, security, availability, maintainability).
keyPoints.implications: Government agencies often neglect non-functional requirements then discover that the fastest vendor solution is unmaintainable or incompatible with agency data governance. Establish security, performance, and operational requirements upfront.

keyPoints.title: Must-Have vs. Nice-to-Have Categorization
keyPoints.description: Distinguishing between mandatory requirements (must have minimum functionality to solve the problem) and desirable features (enhance value but system is acceptable without them). This is critical for evaluation scoring.
keyPoints.implications: Mark requirements clearly in RFP. During evaluation, only use nice-to-have features as differentiators if all proposals meet all must-haves. Prevents evaluation debates about whether proposals really meet requirements.

keyPoints.title: Data and Integration Requirements
keyPoints.description: Government systems rarely operate in isolation. Requirements must address data exchange with other government systems, legacy system integration, and data governance (privacy, security, compliance). DPI assessments often identify hidden integration complexity.
keyPoints.implications: Engage IT infrastructure teams early. Specify data formats, integration interfaces, and compliance requirements explicitly. Consider whether data migration is in-scope (usually adds 6+ months).

keyPoints.title: Stakeholder Involvement in Requirements
keyPoints.description: Requirements gathering for government IT projects must include not just IT leaders but also business process owners, end-users, compliance/legal, and sometimes unions or advocacy groups. Vendor proposals often succeed or fail based on how well they address these diverse stakeholder needs.
keyPoints.implications: Run facilitated requirements workshops. Get sign-off from all stakeholders before finalizing RFP. Build requirements traceability so vendors understand which stakeholder group each requirement serves.

content.keyInsight: Clear, well-organized requirements reduce proposal evaluation time by 30% and reduce post-award scope disputes. Spending an extra month on requirements definition saves 6 months in procurement and contract execution.

exercises.title: Requirements Translation Workshop
exercises.description: Given a business outcome ('Reduce permit processing time by 50%'), develop 5-7 specific requirements that vendors must meet. For each, identify whether it's functional or non-functional, and whether it's must-have or nice-to-have.
exercises.scenario: A state environmental agency wants to modernize its air quality permit system. Currently permits take 6-8 weeks to process. Leadership wants to reduce this to 3-4 weeks. You need to translate this into specific vendor requirements.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Understand that business outcomes require decomposition into specific, measurable requirements. Recognize how to distinguish implementation options from actual requirements.

exercises.title: Identifying Hidden Requirements
exercises.description: Review a draft RFP for a state health IT system. Identify 5 requirements that are implied but not explicitly stated (data security, system availability, integration with federal reporting systems).
exercises.scenario: DPI is assisting with procurement of a system to track communicable disease cases and integrate with federal CDC reporting. The initial RFP focuses on case management workflow but is vague about reporting integration.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Learn to read between the lines in requirements workshops. Identify unstated assumptions that vendors might interpret differently.

content.overview: Designing an RFP that attracts qualified vendors, prevents gaming and subjectivity in evaluation, and complies with government procurement law. The RFP is your primary contractual document during the procurement process—poorly written RFPs lead to expensive protests, poor vendor selection, and downstream contract disputes. DPI advisors often review draft RFPs to identify risks and ambiguities.

keyPoints.title: RFP Structure and Components
keyPoints.description: A complete government RFP typically includes: instructions to vendors (format, submission process, deadlines), requirements sections (functional, non-functional, regulatory), evaluation criteria (with weights and scoring scales), contract terms (standard government clauses), and appendices (forms, technical specs, existing system documentation).
keyPoints.implications: Follow your jurisdiction's RFP template/format to ensure compliance. Include clear instructions so all vendors understand what's expected. Evaluation criteria section is most important—this is what vendors are being judged against.

keyPoints.title: Scoring Rubrics and Evaluation Criteria
keyPoints.description: Define specific evaluation criteria (technical approach, vendor experience, price, schedule) with point values and scoring rules. For qualitative criteria, define scoring levels (excellent = 90-100 pts, good = 70-90, acceptable = 50-70). This prevents subjective arguments during evaluation.
keyPoints.implications: Spend significant time developing rubrics. Test them on 1-2 proposals before using on all proposals. Ensure rubrics map to requirements—every requirement should be evaluated under some criterion.

keyPoints.title: Transparent vs. Sealed Evaluation
keyPoints.description: Some jurisdictions require blind evaluation (evaluators don't know vendor name). Others allow open evaluation. Sealed evaluation reduces bias but can obscure vendor track record. Combination approach: blind technical evaluation, then price/vendor history evaluation after technical scores are set.
keyPoints.implications: Agree on evaluation approach with procurement office before releasing RFP. Document the approach in the RFP to prevent protest claims that process was unfair.

keyPoints.title: Pre-Bid Conferences and Competitive Dialogue
keyPoints.description: Some RFPs include a pre-bid conference where vendors ask clarifying questions. This surfaces ambiguities and ensures all vendors have consistent understanding. Some jurisdictions allow competitive dialogue—iterative feedback with vendors on proposals before final submission.
keyPoints.implications: Pre-bid conferences are low-cost risk reduction. Competitive dialogue is more expensive but much better for complex procurements (enterprise system modernization). Document all Q&A and share with all vendors.

keyPoints.title: Preventing Evaluation Gaming and Protests
keyPoints.description: Common protest triggers: evaluation criteria not applied consistently, requirements changed mid-procurement, price evaluation methodology unclear, vendor claims proposal was technically compliant. Prevention: detailed requirements, clear evaluation criteria, documented decisions, consistent application of rules.
keyPoints.implications: Assume your procurement will be protested. Write everything down. If you deviate from stated process (e.g., allow late submission, waive a requirement for one vendor), document why and be prepared to defend it.

keyPoints.title: Timeline and Communications
keyPoints.description: Typical RFP timeline: 4-6 weeks for pre-procurement planning, 6-8 weeks RFP open period, 4-6 weeks proposal evaluation, 2-4 weeks protest period, then contract negotiation. Total: 16-24 weeks from RFP release to contract award.
keyPoints.implications: Plan accordingly. Start procurement 6+ months before you need the vendor operational. Build in contingency for protests and contract negotiation.

content.keyInsight: The RFP is your communication tool with vendors, your evaluation framework, and your legal document protecting against protests. Invest heavily in RFP quality—a well-written RFP will cost 20-40 hours to prepare, but saves 100+ hours in proposal evaluation and contract negotiation.

exercises.title: Evaluation Rubric Development
exercises.description: Create a detailed scoring rubric for a state IT procurement with four evaluation categories: technical approach (35 pts), vendor experience (20 pts), price (35 pts), and schedule (10 pts). For each category, define 3-4 scoring levels with point ranges and scoring rules.
exercises.scenario: You're evaluating proposals for a new state tax system modernization. You need to balance technical sophistication (don't want vendors to over-engineer), vendor experience (government is risky, want proven vendors), cost (budget is constrained), and schedule (must go live in 18 months).
exercises.expectedOutcome: Learn to translate evaluation criteria into measurable, defensible scoring rules. Understand weighting decisions and their impact on vendor selection.

exercises.title: Ambiguity Detection
exercises.description: Review a 30-page RFP draft. Identify 10 ambiguities, unclear requirements, or gaps that vendors might interpret differently. For each, propose clarifying language.
exercises.scenario: DPI is reviewing an RFP from a state health agency for a new electronic health records system. The RFP mentions '90% system availability' but doesn't specify if this includes planned maintenance. It requires 'modern cloud architecture' but doesn't specify cloud provider options.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Develop skill in reading RFPs from a vendor's perspective. Anticipate ambiguities that lead to protest claims or specification disputes.

exercises.title: RFP Timeline and Milestone Planning
exercises.description: Create a detailed project schedule for an RFP-based government procurement. Start with RFP finalization and include all phases through contract award. Identify critical dependencies and where delays might cascade.
exercises.scenario: Your agency needs a new system operational in 18 months. Work backward to determine when the RFP must be released, considering procurement time, vendor selection, contract negotiation, and implementation planning.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Understand realistic government procurement timelines. Recognize where compressed schedules create risk (tight evaluation windows, limited protest period, rushed contract terms).

content.overview: Evaluating vendor proposals objectively and defensibly. Proposal evaluation is where procurement meets execution. Evaluators must balance vendor marketing narratives with evidence of actual capability. This is also where biases (toward familiar vendors, against smaller vendors) most commonly distort decisions. DPI advisors often participate in evaluation panels to bring independent perspective and rigor.

keyPoints.title: Evaluation Panel Composition and Training
keyPoints.description: Effective evaluation requires 5-7 evaluators with diverse perspectives: business/requirements experts, IT technical experts, procurement specialist, and sometimes external independent evaluator. All must be trained on the evaluation rubric and instructed on avoiding bias (conflict of interest, favoritism toward familiar vendors).
keyPoints.implications: Document who evaluates and their areas of expertise. Require conflict-of-interest disclosures. Use diverse panels to surface different perspectives. External evaluators (like DPI advisors) provide fresh eyes and reduce organizational bias.

keyPoints.title: Proposal Completeness Check
keyPoints.description: Before scoring proposals, verify that each proposal is responsive (addresses all must-have requirements) and compliant (follows RFP submission format, page limits, etc.). Non-responsive proposals should be rejected or vendors given opportunity to correct administrative issues.
keyPoints.implications: Create checklist of RFP requirements. Score completeness before scoring quality. This prevents 'we meant to include that' arguments after proposal submission.

keyPoints.title: Technical Proposal Evaluation
keyPoints.description: Evaluating the vendor's technical approach: Does their architecture solve the stated problem? Is their solution realistic given their team and timeline? Have they addressed all technical requirements? Do they understand integration constraints and data requirements?
keyPoints.implications: Look for depth of understanding, not just buzzwords. A vendor mentioning 'modern microservices architecture' might be parroting marketing versus actually thinking about your specific requirements. Ask follow-up questions during oral presentations.

keyPoints.title: Vendor Experience and References
keyPoints.description: Assessing whether the vendor has successfully delivered similar projects. Government experience is important (vendors unfamiliar with government processes often fail). References from government customers with comparable complexity and budget are most relevant.
keyPoints.implications: Call references. Ask about whether vendor delivered on schedule, stayed within budget, and successfully adapted to requirements changes. Ask about vendor response to problems and relationship management.

keyPoints.title: Price Evaluation Complexity
keyPoints.description: Government price evaluation often uses price reasonableness analysis: Is the proposed price consistent with market rates? Is it suspicious if a vendor is significantly cheaper than others? Sometimes agencies use 'lowest price technically acceptable' (LPTA) where price alone determines winner among compliant proposals.
keyPoints.implications: Understand your jurisdiction's price evaluation rules. Be cautious of unrealistically low bids (indicator of vendor not understanding scope or plan to cut corners). Document price reasonableness analysis.

keyPoints.title: Oral Presentations and Clarification
keyPoints.description: Many government RFPs include vendor oral presentations where vendors present their approach and answer evaluator questions. Presentations reveal whether vendors truly understand the requirements and can articulate their approach clearly.
keyPoints.implications: Require presentations for complex procurements. Develop consistent question sets so all vendors are evaluated on same basis. Presentations often reveal vendor strengths/weaknesses that aren't clear in written proposals.

keyPoints.title: Debasing and Consensus
keyPoints.description: Individual evaluator biases are most likely to affect scoring of subjective criteria (technical approach, vendor approach to requirements). Mitigation: individual evaluators score independently, then group discusses scores and reaches consensus. If scores diverge widely, discuss why.
keyPoints.implications: Don't allow one evaluator's bias to dominate. Use structured deliberation to surface disagreements. Be willing to revise scores if panel discussion reveals new evidence.

content.keyInsight: Proposal evaluation is where most procurement errors occur—weak evaluators missing vendor weaknesses, or strong evaluators ignoring vendor strengths due to organization biases. Invest in evaluation panel quality, use rubrics to enforce consistency, and document decisions thoroughly.

exercises.title: Proposal Evaluation Simulation
exercises.description: Given 3 vendor proposals (redacted/anonymized) for a government IT system, score each using a provided rubric across technical approach, vendor experience, and price. Document your scoring rationale.
exercises.scenario: Three vendors responded to an RFP for a state driver license modernization system: Vendor A (large incumbent contractor, traditional approach), Vendor B (mid-size specialized government contractor, modern approach), Vendor C (small startup, very innovative but limited government experience).
exercises.expectedOutcome: Experience the difficulty of evaluating vendor proposals. Recognize how rubrics guide objective evaluation and prevent subjective 'gut feel' decisions.

exercises.title: Reference Check Protocol
exercises.description: Develop a structured reference check questionnaire for evaluating vendors. Include questions that reveal vendor capabilities, past performance, and ability to respond to problems.
exercises.scenario: Your top-ranked vendor claims experience with government health systems integration. You want to verify this through reference calls with their government customers.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Learn to extract meaningful information from references. Understand what questions differentiate strong vendors from weak ones.

exercises.title: Scoring Consensus and Disagreement
exercises.description: Given a scenario where evaluation panel members scored proposals differently, facilitate a discussion to identify why scores diverged and reach consensus.
exercises.scenario: Three evaluators scored Vendor B's technical proposal as 85, 65, and 75 points. One evaluator thought the approach was innovative; another thought it was risky and unproven for government use.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Learn to facilitate healthy disagreement among evaluators. Understand when to revise scores due to new information versus when to stand by initial assessment.

content.overview: Negotiating contract terms with the selected vendor. Government contracts involve extensive standard legal terms (regulations, compliance, indemnification, liability limitations) plus commercial terms (price, schedule, deliverables, payment terms, incentives). Many government leaders avoid contract negotiation, letting the selected vendor dictate terms. This is a mistake—contract negotiation is where you protect your interests and set expectations for the vendor relationship.

keyPoints.title: Government Contract Standard Terms
keyPoints.description: Government contracts include standard terms mandated by law or regulation: clauses on compliance with federal labor laws, environmental regulations, civil rights, and accessibility standards. These terms are often non-negotiable. What's negotiable: performance requirements, delivery schedule, payment terms, liability limitations, change order procedures, termination provisions.
keyPoints.implications: Separate mandatory terms from negotiable terms before negotiation. Accept government standard terms that protect taxpayer interests. Negotiate hard on performance and schedule terms.

keyPoints.title: Defining Deliverables, Acceptance, and Payment
keyPoints.description: Contracts must specify what vendor will deliver (technical specifications), acceptance criteria (how you determine if deliverables meet requirements), and payment terms (when you pay). Government contracts often use milestone-based payment: vendor delivers milestone, you inspect, you approve, then you pay.
keyPoints.implications: Detailed deliverables definitions prevent disputes. Clear acceptance criteria prevent vendor delivery of substandard work. Milestone payment protects government cash flow and incentivizes vendor performance.

keyPoints.title: Performance Metrics and Incentives
keyPoints.description: Contracts can include performance metrics (system uptime, response time) with financial incentives (bonuses for exceeding targets) or penalties (price reductions if metrics not met). Some government contracts use fixed price (vendor bears risk) versus time-and-materials (government bears risk).
keyPoints.implications: Use fixed price contracts for well-defined work (implementation of specified requirements). Use time-and-materials for uncertain/exploratory work. Align contract terms with risk allocation.

keyPoints.title: Change Order Process
keyPoints.description: Government projects almost always require scope changes (new requirements, changed requirements, discovered complexity). Contracts must specify the change order process: how changes are requested, evaluated, approved, and priced. Without clear change procedures, scope creep is inevitable.
keyPoints.implications: Establish clear change procedures upfront. Require detailed change impact analysis (schedule, budget) before approving changes. Control change requests to prevent runaway scope.

keyPoints.title: Termination and Exit Provisions
keyPoints.description: Government contracts must address what happens if vendor fails to perform (termination for cause) or if government cancels contract (termination for convenience). Provisions specify vendor obligations at termination (data delivery, IP rights, settlement), government payment obligations, and notice periods.
keyPoints.implications: Ensure contracts allow termination for convenience if vendor performance is unacceptable. Require vendor to deliver data/work product at termination. This protects government from being locked into failing vendor relationship.

keyPoints.title: Vendor Negotiating Tactics and Pushback
keyPoints.description: Vendors often push back on contract terms: requesting higher payment, shorter milestones, lower liability, limited warranty. Vendors especially resist government standard terms (compliance, accessibility, security). Understanding vendor pressure points helps you negotiate effectively.
keyPoints.implications: Distinguish between vendor objections that have merit (timeline is truly unrealistic) versus resistance to reasonable terms (standard government compliance clauses). Be willing to adjust timeline/price to accommodate reasonable vendor concerns. Stand firm on government protections.

keyPoints.title: Multi-Vendor Relationships and Subcontracting
keyPoints.description: Large government projects often involve multiple vendors (prime contractor and subcontractors). Contracts must specify vendor's role, responsibilities, and relationship to other contractors. Prime contractor accountability to government is important.
keyPoints.implications: For complex procurements with multiple vendors, establish clear role definitions and interface requirements. Ensure prime contractor is responsible for overall delivery and subcontractor coordination.

content.keyInsight: Contract negotiation is not adversarial—it's aligning vendor and government interests. Well-negotiated contracts prevent disputes, establish clear expectations, and create foundation for successful vendor relationship. Vendors respect government organizations that negotiate professionally and hold to terms they've committed to.

exercises.title: Contract Term Prioritization
exercises.description: Given a list of 20 contract terms to negotiate (payment schedule, milestone definitions, performance metrics, termination provisions, change order process, warranty, liability, subcontracting restrictions, etc.), prioritize which are most important for your specific procurement.
exercises.scenario: You're negotiating a fixed-price IT system implementation contract with a selected vendor. The vendor has asked for changes to several standard government terms. You have limited negotiation bandwidth.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Learn to distinguish essential contract terms from negotiable details. Understand how to prioritize negotiations to focus on terms most critical to project success.

exercises.title: Milestone Definition and Acceptance Criteria
exercises.description: Define 5-7 milestones for a 12-month IT implementation project, with specific deliverables and acceptance criteria for each milestone. Include payment schedule.
exercises.scenario: A state agency is contracting with a vendor to implement a new case management system. The vendor proposal shows 4 phases: requirements finalization, design, development, and testing/go-live. You need to establish measurable milestones with clear acceptance criteria so you know when to pay.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Develop skill in translating project phases into contract milestones. Understand how clear acceptance criteria prevent disputes about whether vendor has performed.

exercises.title: Change Order Process Development
exercises.description: Design a change order process for a government IT contract: how changes are requested, how impact is assessed, who approves changes, how changes are priced, and how schedule/budget are adjusted.
exercises.scenario: During implementation of a new benefits system, the state identifies additional integration points with federal systems that weren't captured in original requirements. This will add 2 months and $500K to the contract. You need a fair process to evaluate and approve this change.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Learn to establish change control that protects government interests while acknowledging that changes are inevitable in government IT projects.

content.overview: Managing vendors after contract award to ensure they perform as promised. Vendor management includes monitoring progress against milestones, managing communications and escalations, enforcing contract terms, and maintaining positive working relationship. Many government leaders incorrectly believe their role ends when the contract is signed. In fact, active vendor management is what determines whether the project succeeds or fails.

keyPoints.title: Establishing Vendor Management Governance
keyPoints.description: Effective vendor management requires clear governance: who is the vendor account manager? Who approves changes? Who escalates issues? What is the cadence of status reviews and steering committee meetings? Government organizations should establish vendor governance that mirrors their internal project governance.
keyPoints.implications: Assign dedicated person to manage vendor relationship. Establish weekly status meetings for implementation projects, monthly reviews for operations contracts. Escalate significant issues (schedule slippage, budget overruns, quality problems) to senior leadership promptly.

keyPoints.title: Monitoring Progress and Deliverables
keyPoints.description: Government should not passively wait for vendor to deliver. Active monitoring includes: weekly status calls, review of draft deliverables, assessment of whether milestones will be met on time and on budget, early identification of risks and issues. Government team should understand vendor's work plan in detail.
keyPoints.implications: Don't accept summary status ('on schedule'). Dig into details. Review actual work product, not just vendor reports. Establish clear indicators of progress (number of requirements implemented, percentage of design complete, test cases executed). Early visibility of problems allows time to address them.

keyPoints.title: Issue Identification and Escalation
keyPoints.description: Problems emerge during vendor management: requirements are misunderstood, schedule slips, vendor resources are inadequate, technical issues arise. Early problem identification and escalation prevents surprises. Vendors sometimes hide problems hoping to solve them later.
keyPoints.implications: Create safe space for vendors to raise issues without fear of penalty. Escalate issues promptly to steering committee. When vendor identifies problem, evaluate: Is this vendor problem (vendor should fix) or government problem (scope change)? Address root cause, not just symptoms.

keyPoints.title: Contract Enforcement and Remedies
keyPoints.description: If vendor fails to meet contract terms (late milestones, poor quality, non-compliance with requirements), government must enforce contract terms. Options: withhold payment pending correction, apply liquidated damages (financial penalties), request corrective action plan, or terminate contract. Knowing when and how to enforce keeps vendors accountable.
keyPoints.implications: Document failures. Give vendor opportunity to cure (fix problem) before applying penalties. Use escalation path: first address in technical meetings, then vendor management escalation, then executive escalation, then legal action. Most vendors will correct problems when issue is escalated appropriately.

keyPoints.title: Maintaining Effective Communications
keyPoints.description: Vendor management depends on clear, consistent communication. Weekly status meetings should address: progress toward milestones, identified risks/issues, decisions needed, upcoming activities. Documentation should be clear: meeting minutes capture decisions, action items, and owners.
keyPoints.implications: Over-communicate rather than under-communicate. Written communication (emails, meeting minutes) creates accountability. Verbal-only communication leads to misunderstanding and finger-pointing.

keyPoints.title: Vendor Performance Evaluation and Relationship Management
keyPoints.description: Periodically evaluate vendor performance against contract terms and performance metrics. This evaluation may affect payment (performance incentives/penalties), renewal decisions, or relationship adjustments. Vendors are motivated by both enforcement and recognition when they perform well.
keyPoints.implications: Establish formal performance evaluation process (quarterly or at project milestones). Document positive and negative performance. Use evaluations to support decisions about future vendor engagement.

keyPoints.title: Managing Multiple Vendors and Dependencies
keyPoints.description: Large government projects often involve multiple vendors working together. Vendor management complexity increases significantly: coordinating between vendors, managing interdependencies, ensuring integration works, addressing disputes between vendors.
keyPoints.implications: Assign clear integration authority (usually prime contractor or government program manager). Establish clear interfaces and integration requirements. Schedule coordination meetings between vendors. Escalate vendor disputes promptly.

content.keyInsight: Vendor management is where contracts come to life. Proactive vendor management—establishing clear governance, monitoring progress, escalating issues, and maintaining communication—determines whether vendors perform as promised. Government leaders who delegate vendor management to junior staff often discover too late that projects are failing.

exercises.title: Vendor Status Review Facilitation
exercises.description: Role-play facilitating a vendor status review meeting where the vendor reports schedule slippage on key milestones. The vendor blames government for late requirements decisions; government believes vendor underestimated effort. Conduct the meeting to identify root cause and establish corrective action.
exercises.scenario: Your IT implementation vendor reports they'll be 6 weeks late on the design phase milestone. They cite two factors: government took 4 weeks to approve final requirements (versus 2 weeks planned), and discovery conversations revealed more integration complexity than anticipated.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Learn to separate vendor accountability from legitimate external factors. Understand how to facilitate discussion of problems without being defensive. Develop corrective actions that address root causes.

exercises.title: Vendor Governance and Escalation Framework
exercises.description: Design a vendor governance structure for a 2-year, $5M IT implementation project with 3 vendors (prime + 2 subs). Include: governance roles, meeting structure, decision authorities, and escalation path for issues.
exercises.scenario: You're responsible for vendor management on a major government modernization initiative. You need to establish clear governance so issues are resolved at appropriate level and don't cascade into major problems.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Develop understanding of governance structures that support vendor accountability and effective problem resolution.

exercises.title: Performance Metric Tracking
exercises.description: Establish a performance dashboard for tracking a vendor's performance against contract terms. Include metrics for schedule (on-time milestones), budget (cost tracking), quality (defects, rework), and customer satisfaction.
exercises.scenario: You want to monitor your vendor's performance objectively. You've defined contract milestones and performance metrics in the contract. Now you need a system to track whether vendor is meeting those metrics.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Learn to establish objective metrics that reveal vendor performance trends and enable data-driven management decisions.

content.overview: Addressing vendor performance problems and managing the path to either vendor improvement or vendor replacement. Not all vendors perform well. Some fail to meet schedules, deliver poor quality work, or struggle with government requirements. Government leaders must have strategies for addressing vendor failures while protecting project continuity. DPI often helps agencies navigate difficult vendor situations including terminations and transition to alternative vendors.

keyPoints.title: Early Warning Signs of Vendor Problems
keyPoints.description: Vendor problems rarely appear as sudden failures. Warning signs: missed status updates, vague status reports, turnover of key vendor staff, schedule slippage early in project, rework of work already approved, vendor not responding to requests, changes in vendor financial stability.
keyPoints.implications: Monitor actively for warning signs. When signs appear, escalate immediately rather than hoping vendor will self-correct. Early intervention prevents failures from becoming catastrophic.

keyPoints.title: Root Cause Analysis for Vendor Problems
keyPoints.description: When problems emerge, determine root cause: Is vendor underperforming due to lack of capability (wrong vendor), insufficient resources (vendor took on too much work), miscommunication about requirements, or changed circumstances (scope creep, requirements changes)?
keyPoints.implications: Root cause analysis determines solution: capability problem might require vendor replacement; resource problem might be fixed by vendor adding staff; requirements miscommunication might require clarification. Different root causes require different solutions.

keyPoints.title: Corrective Action Plans and Vendor Improvement
keyPoints.description: When vendor is underperforming, government can require corrective action plan: vendor identifies root cause, proposes fixes, commits to specific improvements, and accepts monitoring/oversight. For example: vendor adds senior resources, implements different development methodology, or increases status reporting frequency.
keyPoints.implications: Require corrective action plan when problems are identified. Monitor plan execution closely. If improvements aren't visible within agreed timeframe, escalate to vendor replacement.

keyPoints.title: Performance Remedies: Payment Withholding and Liquidated Damages
keyPoints.description: Contracts typically include performance remedies: withhold payment pending corrective action (most common), apply liquidated damages (contractual penalties for late delivery or poor quality). Using remedies signals government seriousness about performance while incentivizing improvement.
keyPoints.implications: Use payment withholding as last resort—it can drive vendor into financial crisis which makes performance worse. Apply liquidated damages according to contract terms. Communicate to vendor why remedies are being applied (what specific failures triggered them).

keyPoints.title: Vendor Replacement and Transition Planning
keyPoints.description: If corrective actions fail or vendor is incapable, government must replace vendor. Transition planning includes: identify replacement vendor (existing contractor, emergency procurement, bring work in-house), transfer work product and knowledge, establish transition timeline, plan for work continuity.
keyPoints.implications: Vendor replacement is expensive and time-consuming. Use it as last resort. When replacement is necessary, transition planning is critical—hasty transition often creates larger problems than original vendor failure.

keyPoints.title: Termination for Cause vs. Termination for Convenience
keyPoints.description: Contracts distinguish between termination for cause (vendor materially breaches contract, grounds for legal action) and termination for convenience (government decides to end contract regardless of vendor performance). Termination for convenience is often easier legally, though may trigger vendor claims.
keyPoints.implications: Use termination for cause when vendor materially fails (quality is dangerous, never meets milestones, doesn't comply with requirements). Use termination for convenience when you lose confidence but don't have clear breach. Be prepared for vendor to dispute termination decision.

keyPoints.title: Managing Vendor Disputes and Escalation
keyPoints.description: Vendor problems sometimes escalate into formal disputes: vendor claims government is responsible for delays, government claims vendor is underperforming, vendor denies they breached contract. Disputes can go to vendor management, then executive leadership, then mediation, then litigation.
keyPoints.implications: Exhaustively document vendor performance issues before escalating to dispute. Include communications with vendor about problems and opportunities to improve. Well-documented issues support government position in disputes.

content.keyInsight: Vendor problems are inevitable in large government projects. Leaders who address problems early, root cause analysis, and escalate appropriately prevent small problems from becoming catastrophic failures. Conversely, leaders who ignore vendor warning signs and delay addressing problems often find themselves in crisis remediation.

exercises.title: Early Warning Signs Scenario
exercises.description: Given a vendor status report and communication history, identify 5-7 early warning signs that vendor is struggling. What indicators suggest problems are emerging?
exercises.scenario: Review 6 months of status reports and emails from your IT implementation vendor. Status reports are becoming increasingly vague. Key technical lead was recently replaced. Two meetings in a row were rescheduled at last minute. Vendor is asking for timeline extension 'to ensure quality'.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Develop sensitivity to warning signs that precede vendor failures. Understand how to recognize problems before they become visible in missed milestones.

exercises.title: Root Cause Analysis and Corrective Action
exercises.description: Given a vendor problem scenario, conduct root cause analysis and develop a corrective action plan. Determine whether problem stems from vendor capability, resource constraints, or other factors.
exercises.scenario: Your state health system vendor delivered a system design that doesn't align with requirements. The design uses outdated architecture patterns and doesn't address integration complexity you discussed. Is this a capability problem, a communication problem, or something else? What corrective action would address root cause?
exercises.expectedOutcome: Learn diagnostic process for vendor problems. Understand how different root causes require different corrective actions.

exercises.title: Vendor Replacement Planning
exercises.description: Develop a transition plan for replacing an underperforming vendor mid-project. Assume project is 40% complete and requires 12 more months. New vendor needs to understand existing work and continue forward.
exercises.scenario: Your IT vendor is 3 months behind schedule and quality of delivered code is below standards. You've requested corrective action twice. You've decided to replace them. Plan the transition: how do you transfer the work, ensure continuity, and prevent further delay?
exercises.expectedOutcome: Understand complexity of vendor replacement and why transition planning is critical. Recognize that replacement is expensive and should be used only after other remedies fail.

content.overview: Developing long-term vendor strategies beyond individual procurements. Strategic vendor management involves building stable vendor ecosystem that supports government modernization objectives. This includes vendor diversity (avoiding over-reliance on single vendors), vendor development (helping smaller/newer vendors enter government market), and collaborative partnerships (joint improvement initiatives with key vendors). DPI helps government agencies think beyond individual projects to develop coherent vendor strategies aligned with modernization goals.

keyPoints.title: Vendor Concentration vs. Competition
keyPoints.description: Government IT markets often have limited competition. Some states have 1-2 vendors dominating certain service categories (systems integration, cloud services, staffing). Vendor concentration reduces competition, drives up prices, and can limit innovation. Strategies to increase competition: unbundle large procurements to enable smaller vendors, set-asides for minority-owned/small businesses, invest in vendor capability development.
keyPoints.implications: Monitor vendor market concentration. When few vendors dominate, take deliberate steps to create opportunities for new competitors. Over time, competition drives better outcomes and lower costs.

keyPoints.title: Small Business and Diversity Vendor Development
keyPoints.description: Many government IT markets are dominated by large firms. Smaller and minority-owned vendors often lack resources to compete in large government procurements. Strategies to develop diverse vendor ecosystem: joint ventures with large primes, subcontracting targets, apprenticeships/training programs, and small-dollar procurements to build track record.
keyPoints.implications: Deliberate investment in diverse vendors strengthens market, creates local business opportunities, and often produces better solutions (smaller vendors more nimble, more responsive). Aligns with government social equity goals.

keyPoints.title: Preferred Vendor Relationships and Strategic Partnerships
keyPoints.description: Beyond individual transactional procurements, government can develop preferred vendor relationships: vendors that have consistently performed well, understand government requirements, and align with agency modernization strategy. These vendors might participate in planning, provide input on new initiatives, and serve as trusted advisors.
keyPoints.implications: Preferred vendors reduce procurement time and risk (known capability, track record). But can also reduce competition if not balanced with open procurements. Use preferred vendor relationships for non-competitive work (consulting, advisory services) and require competitive procurement for major system implementations.

keyPoints.title: Vendor Ecosystem Mapping and Capability Assessment
keyPoints.description: Strategic vendor management starts with understanding your vendor ecosystem: which vendors serve which domains, what capabilities exist or are missing, where are competitive markets vs. monopolies. DPI conducts vendor ecosystem assessments as part of modernization planning.
keyPoints.implications: Regular vendor ecosystem assessment reveals gaps (missing capabilities) and concentrations (vendor over-reliance). Identifies where intentional vendor development is needed to support modernization strategy.

keyPoints.title: Joint Improvement and Innovation Partnerships
keyPoints.description: Some government agencies work with vendors on joint improvement initiatives: innovation labs, pilot programs, shared problem-solving. These partnerships generate new solutions and deepen vendor understanding of government needs.
keyPoints.implications: Collaborative partnerships with vendors (beyond transactional procurement) can accelerate innovation. But require careful governance to prevent favoritism and maintain competitive balance.

keyPoints.title: Contract Consolidation and Unbundling Strategies
keyPoints.description: Government can influence vendor market structure through contracting strategy: consolidation (combine multiple services into single large contract to create efficiency) or unbundling (break large service into smaller contracts to enable smaller vendors). Each approach has trade-offs.
keyPoints.implications: Consolidation reduces contract overhead and can leverage economies of scale, but can also create large contracts only major vendors can pursue. Unbundling creates opportunities for smaller vendors but can create integration complexity. Choose strategy aligned with modernization objectives.

keyPoints.title: Managing Vendor Relationships and Expectations
keyPoints.description: Long-term vendor relationships require relationship management: regular business reviews, honest conversations about performance and expectations, feedback on what's working and what's not. Government leaders who treat vendors as partners (not just contractors) tend to get better outcomes.
keyPoints.implications: Regular vendor relationship reviews (quarterly or annually) create feedback loops that improve performance. Vendors who understand government's goals and feel respected tend to be more innovative and flexible when problems arise.

content.keyInsight: Strategic vendor management extends beyond individual procurements to ecosystem development. Government agencies that intentionally develop diverse, competitive vendor ecosystems achieve better outcomes: lower costs, more innovation, faster execution, and stronger alignment with modernization strategy.

exercises.title: Vendor Ecosystem Assessment
exercises.description: Analyze your government's current IT vendor ecosystem. Map major vendors by service category (systems integration, cloud infrastructure, staffing, security). Identify which categories have strong competition vs. monopoly/duopoly vendors. Assess where vendor capability gaps exist.
exercises.scenario: You're advising a state government on modernization strategy. You need to understand current vendor ecosystem to identify where market concentration is limiting options and where new vendors should be developed to support modernization objectives.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Understand how to assess vendor ecosystem strategically. Recognize how vendor competition and diversity affects government's ability to accomplish modernization.

exercises.title: Vendor Diversity and Development Strategy
exercises.description: Develop a strategy to increase small and minority-owned business participation in government IT procurements. Consider: where are there barriers to entry? How can government create opportunities for new vendors?
exercises.scenario: Analysis reveals that IT system integration work is dominated by 3 large firms. Only 2% of contracts go to small/minority-owned vendors. You want to increase diversity while maintaining quality and not increasing costs. Design a vendor development strategy.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Learn how to balance competitive, cost-effective procurement with vendor diversity goals. Understand various mechanisms (small-dollar contracts, joint ventures, apprenticeships) to develop diverse vendors.

exercises.title: Strategic Vendor Relationship Planning
exercises.description: Identify one of your organization's key IT vendors. Develop a strategic relationship plan: quarterly business reviews, feedback mechanisms, joint improvement initiatives, communication protocol. How will you maintain relationship while keeping procurement competitive?
exercises.scenario: Your organization has worked with the same systems integrator for 5 years across multiple projects. They've performed well and understand your organization's needs. You want to develop deeper strategic relationship while maintaining healthy vendor competition and preventing over-reliance.
exercises.expectedOutcome: Understand how to develop strategic vendor partnerships in context of competitive procurement. Recognize balance between preferred vendor convenience and market competition.
